To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the personality traits of neuroticism and extraversion were associated with willingness to volunteer for experiments.

(1) extraversion and neurotiscm are related to willingness to volunteer for an experiment, and (2) high extraversion and high neuroticism are both associated with willingness to volunteer for a shock experiment.
extraverted and neurotic individuals volunteer more for experiments than introverts and stable individuals.

the personality characteristics of volunteer subjects.
the relationship between personality and volunteering for experiments.
the personality characteristics of the volunteers and nonvolunteers in the laboratory.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
extraversion is a significant factor in volunteering for experiments, and neuroticism is a significant factor only for shock experiments.
extraverts are more likely to volunteer for a study if the study is perceived as being more interesting and/or more social.
the personality differences found are in accordance with the Eysenckian model of extraversion and neurosis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use personality to understand how individuals will behave in different situations.
we have shown that it is possible to use a single experiment to study a wide range of personality traits, which is not possible with traditional personality tests.
the use of volunteer participants in psychological research may lead to the selection of individuals who are not representative of the general population.
